text: The fortnight had come and gone without incident, which had done considerably less to ease anyone's nerves than a genuine attack might have, if only because a threat that fails to arrive on schedule has an unpleasant habit of feeling more patient rather than less real.

“He's taking his time,” Will observed, for perhaps the fourth time that week, watching Marian and Thistlewood conclude another of their brief, unexplained consultations near the fire. “I don't know whether that's good news or considerably worse news dressed up politely.”
“Worse, generally,” said Grimalkin, from Marian's shoulders, to no ears but the animals' own. “Men who take their time have usually decided the waiting itself is part of the plan.”
“Cheerful,” said Barley.
“I never claimed to be Crumb,” said Grimalkin.

It was Wat who broke the uneasy quiet, arriving at speed with Hob close behind him, both boys wearing the particular grim urgency that had, by now, become an entirely reliable predictor of bad news arriving shortly after they did.
“Ellen sent us,” Wat said, catching his breath. “Said it couldn't wait for a proper messenger this time.”
“What's happened?” Robin asked, already on his feet.

“The muster's moving,” Hob said. “Properly moving. Not gathering anymore — marching. There's a captain leading the first of it into Sherwood itself, and word is she's nothing at all like the men you've dealt with so far.”

sequence._describe: Wat Hale and Hob Weaver delivering urgent grim news to the gathered crew, Marian Fletcher listening with careful attention, Long John Little visibly uneasy, tension rising. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. text: “A captain,” Marian repeated, already turning the word over with the particular care she gave anything that might matter more than it first appeared to. “Not the Sheriff himself, then. Not yet.”

“Not yet,” Wat agreed. “Captain Rowena Blackwood, they're calling her. Ellen's contacts say she's proper army — fought in the north before the Sheriff bought her contract, not some tax farmer's hired muscle playing at soldiering. Disciplined. Patient. Doesn't lose men to carelessness, on account of never being careless herself.”
“That's not encouraging,” said Long John, quietly.
“It's not meant to be,” said Hob. “Ellen wanted you to know exactly what's coming. Said you'd rather have the truth of it than a comfortable version.”
“How many with her?” Marian asked.

“Enough,” said Wat, which was, of all the answers available to a nine-year-old relaying secondhand information, probably the most honest one he could have given. “More than the search party. Fewer than a full army, from what Ellen's contacts could tell. She's not here to conquer Sherwood outright. She's here to find you properly, and hold ground until the rest of what the Sheriff's building can follow.”
Brother Crumb, who had been unusually quiet through the whole exchange, finally spoke. “A scouting force with teeth, then. Softening the ground before the real weight arrives.”
“That's precisely it,” said Thistlewood, grim, from where he'd been listening without comment. “I'd hoped we'd have longer.”

sequence._describe: The crew planning a scouting mission, Marian Fletcher laying out the plan with resolve, Will Scarlett-Sleeves checking his sleeve, Pip standing nearby with quiet determination. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, focused daytime camp lighting, resolute mood.

text: “We should see her for ourselves,” Marian said, once the shape of the danger had settled enough to make room for planning. “Not engage. Just see. I'd rather know precisely what we're facing than build a plan around secondhand descriptions, however good Ellen's sources are.”
“Agreed,” said Robin, with more steadiness in his voice than he'd quite expected to find there. “Small group. Quiet. We look, we learn, we come home.”

“That's a sensible plan,” said Will, checking his sleeve with the particular thoroughness of a man bracing for something he intended to look presentable for regardless. “I don't trust it to survive contact with the enemy, but it's sensible.”
“I'm coming,” Pip said, quietly, in the tone of someone who had already decided the matter and was simply extending the courtesy of announcing it rather than asking permission.

Marian glanced at her, then at Thistlewood, and found in his small, resigned nod exactly the confirmation she'd expected. “Then we go together. Quietly. No one does anything clever without saying so first.”
“Will's going to do something clever,” Long John observed.
“I resent that,” said Will, “on the grounds that it's almost certainly accurate.”

sequence._describe: The scouting party observing Captain Rowena Blackwood's disciplined military column from a hidden ridge, Blackwood in plain functional armor at the head of organized troops, a genuine step up in competence from anything faced before. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, tense daytime forest overlook lighting, serious observant mood.

text: What they found, from the cover of a low ridge overlooking the approaching column, was considerably more unsettling than any of Ellen's secondhand descriptions had quite managed to convey. The men below moved with the crisp, unhurried precision of soldiers who trained together rather than simply served alongside one another — no straggling, no idle chatter, tents struck and re-raised with a speed that spoke of long practice rather than urgency.

At the column's head rode a woman in plain, functional armor, entirely without the ornamentation men like Vane seemed unable to resist — sharp-eyed, upright, giving orders in a voice pitched to carry exactly as far as it needed to and no further.
“That's her,” Marian said, quietly. “Blackwood.”

They watched a long while, cataloguing what they could — the column's pace, its discipline, the particular efficiency with which Blackwood's scouts fanned out and returned, reporting in clipped, economical exchanges that gave away nothing to anyone not already standing close enough to hear them.
“She's good,” Robin said, finally, with the reluctant respect of a man recognizing genuine competence even in an enemy. “Properly good. Not like the others.”

“No,” Marian agreed. “Which means we stop treating this the way we've treated everything else. Luck and improvisation got us through tax men and highwaymen and a vain fool with a strongbox. It will not get us through her.”

“She's noticed the birds have gone quiet,” Grimalkin observed, low, watching Blackwood's head turn fractionally toward their ridge with unsettling precision. “That's not luck either. That's someone who actually pays attention.”

sequence._describe: The scouting party carefully withdrawing through the forest, unease and resolve on their faces, the weight of the new threat settling in, Thistlewood glancing back toward the distant column. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, muted late-afternoon forest lighting, heavy contemplative mood.

text: They withdrew carefully, unseen — or unseen as far as any of them could tell, which was, given what they'd just watched, considerably less reassuring a thought than it would have been a week earlier — and didn't speak again properly until they were well clear of the ridge and the column both.
“So,” said Will, eventually, into the heavy quiet. “That's the shape of it, then.”

“That's the shape of it,” Marian agreed. “A real soldier, leading real soldiers, and considerably more patience than anyone we've faced so far. This isn't a search party we can misdirect with a beehive and good luck.”
Pip, walking close beside her, said nothing for a long moment, then added, quietly: “It isn't the end of anything. Just the beginning of the part that actually matters.”

“No,” Thistlewood agreed, grim but steady, “I don't imagine it is.” He looked back once, toward the distant column now lost behind the trees, and there was something in his expression — old, weary, and entirely without his usual dry humor — that none of them had quite seen on him before. “Well. We'd best begin properly, then. All of us.”
